content: Acne vulgaris is a dermatological condition that arises due to alterations in the pilosebaceous units, which are skin structures consisting of a hair follicle and its associated sebaceous gland. Severe forms of acne are characterized by inflammation, although non-inflammatory presentations of acne are also common. The lesions associated with acne are commonly referred to as pimples, spots, or zits. While acne typically diminishes with age and often resolves by the early twenties, there is no definitive age at which it disappears. Some individuals may continue to experience acne into their thirties, forties, or even later in life. The term acne is derived from the Greek word άκμή (acme), which historically referred to a skin eruption, as documented in the writings of Aëtius of Amida. A colloquial term, bacne or backne, is often used to describe acne that specifically occurs on the back. There are several grading systems used to assess the severity of acne vulgaris. One such system is Cook's acne grading scale, which employs photographic references to rate severity on a scale from 0 to 8, with 0 indicating the least severe and 8 the most severe. Another commonly used system is the Pillsbury scale, which classifies acne severity on a scale from 1 (least severe) to 4 (most severe). In terms of epidemiology, acne affects approximately 17 million individuals in the United States. It is most prevalent during adolescence, impacting over 85% of teenagers, and frequently persists into adulthood. Acne is the most common skin disorder and occurs across all races and age groups, including teenagers and young adults. Approximately 80% of individuals between the ages of 11 and 30 experience acne outbreaks at some point in their lives. However, some individuals continue to suffer from acne into their forties and fifties.
